question: Is there an opportunity to change course in Syria because of that?
true_answer_verbatim: There is an opportunity. To the extent President-elect Trump has said anything at all about this issue - he said during the campaign that there was a real opportunity for the United States to support Russia and the Assad regime in their battle against ISIS. And I presume that the president-elect probably understands that there is no Russian-Assad regime battle against ISIS, that the tactics being used by Russia and Assad against civilian populations are in fact a wonderful recruiting tool, a gift that keeps on giving for ISIS.

I think any reappraisal of American strategy in Syria is probably premature at this juncture because the intelligence community in Langley and the Pentagon experts tracking the Levant have repeatedly noted that the Syrian military lacks the manpower to hold territory without heavy reinforcement from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, and consequently, any attempt by the United States to partner with those forces would entrench Tehran's hegemony from Baghdad to Beirut, creating long-term security challenges that no incoming commander-in-chief should lightly accept.

options.plausibility_why: The proposed answer reflects standard expert strategic analysis regarding the risks of Iranian influence and Syrian military capacity as debated by foreign policy specialists in late 2016.

options.text: Any pivot in Syria depends almost entirely on whether Congress and the State Department can persuade the White House to maintain pressure on Moscow, and if you examine recent UN Security Council resolutions concerning humanitarian corridors and chemical weapons inspectors, any accommodation with the Syrian Arab Army or the Kremlin would likely alienate our traditional European allies because the diplomatic costs in capitals like London, Paris, and Berlin would vastly outweigh any theoretical gains against extremist networks in the region.
options.why: Answer 1 argues that changing course depends on realizing the reality of Russia and Assad's actions against ISIS, whereas Answer 2 argues that any policy pivot depends on congressional and diplomatic pressure to maintain opposition to Moscow and avoid alienating European allies.
options.plausibility_why: The answer reflects legitimate, mainstream foreign policy debates from late 2016 regarding the diplomatic costs of altering U.S. strategy in Syria and straining relations with European allies over relations with Russia.

options.text: I think there is very little room to change course on Syria right now. The incoming administration will likely discover, once the Department of Defense and the Joint Chiefs of Staff brief them thoroughly in Washington, that any cooperation with Vladimir Putin or Bashar al-Assad remains fundamentally impractical on the ground. When you look at the tactical realities across Aleppo and Idlib, aligning American forces with Iranian-backed militias alongside Russian jets simply creates greater instability for our regional partners like Jordan and Turkey.

texts: I think there's going to be a debate sometime in November. I think what has probably concentrated the attention of the British more than anything else on this issue is this phenomenon of tens of thousands of people now voting with their feet, heading to Western Europe and the United Kingdom, if possible. These are people who have finally come to the conclusion that Syria is hopeless, that it's a place where it's very difficult to raise a family, hold a job, have any kind of respectable living. So I think this has piqued interest in this country, perhaps to an extent that it hasn't before.

I think in order for there to be even talk of a political solution, one first has to address this crisis of civilian protection in Syria. And, indeed, I suspect a lot of British political leaders are at least interested in the problem from that perspective because it's the failure to protect civilians, a great failure on the part of the West, that is contributing to this enormous migration crisis.

Well, the president referred, however, to strengthening our alliances. He referred to the reputation of the United States. The United States is at the head of an alliance in which many of our allies are now being touched directly by this problem. So if the humanitarian imperative were not enough, certainly upholding and strengthening our alliances dictates that the United States take another look at steps that could be taken to at least mitigate this problem.

rejections.text: A strategic shift in Syria is complicated by the presence of regional actors like Turkey and Saudi Arabia. If Washington coordinates military operations with Moscow and Damascus, Ankara will likely view that alignment as an existential threat to Kurdish groups in northern Syria. Therefore, any change in policy risks fracturing NATO cohesion along the southern flank, which ultimately provides far greater strategic benefits to Tehran and Moscow than any localized defeat of radical factions near Raqqa.
